title: No hot wind touches
hookLine: no hot wind touches the one in the Lord's refuge (Bilaval M5, ang 819)

cards: In a Punjabi June, the afternoon wind doesn't cool you. It burns. It comes off the plains like the air from an open oven, and people have a name for it: the loo.
Shops pull their shutters, farmers rest under the trees, and mothers keep children indoors until evening. Where that wind blows, shade isn't a nice extra. It's survival.
Guru Arjan turned that experience into a line of comfort.

teach.b: The shabad is in Raag Bilaval, on Ang eight nineteen, and it opens: taatee vaao na lagaee, paarbraham sarnaaee. In paraphrase: the hot wind doesn't touch the one who is in the refuge of the Supreme Lord.
Then the picture widens. All around me, on four sides, is the Lord's protective circle, so no pain touches me. I met the true Guru, who made this happen; he gave me the medicine of the Lord's Name.
Three images hold it together. Taatee vaao, the hot wind, stands for whatever scorches: illness, fear, cruelty, grief.
Sarnaaee is refuge, sanctuary, the place you run to.
And the circle on four sides is a line drawn around you, a protected space, a boundary harm can't cross. Then the last image quietly answers a hard question.
The Guru gives a medicine, aukhadh: the Name. Nobody hands medicine to someone who is perfectly well. So the shabad doesn't picture a life where nothing ever scorches.
It pictures someone who has been given what heals, with a line drawn around them while the wind blows.
It is sung in hospital rooms, before journeys, when a baby is born, or simply at night. It isn't a charm. It's shade and medicine, held out together.

how: Sikhs often sing or recite taatee vaao na lagaee for protection and comfort: at a birth, before travel, in illness, or at bedtime.

o: a storm sent as a punishment
a cool breeze after summer rain

games.q: the hot wind — tap the pairs.
p: the Name, given by the Guru

s: the shabad calls the Name a medicine
the true Guru gave the medicine of the Lord's Name.
taatee vaao means a cool breeze
it's the hot wind, the kind that scorches.

games.q: the loo is blowing outside and a friend is in the hospital. what does the shabad's picture offer?
o: a refuge: a circle on four sides that the hot wind can't cross.
games.why: the shabad pictures the Lord's protective circle, and the Name as medicine: shade on the inside while the wind blows.

practice: Move, if you can, to the coolest, quietest spot near you, or simply close your eyes, and name one hot wind blowing in your life right now. Then picture a circle drawn around you on four sides, and rest inside it.
If you pray, say Waheguru, or the shabad's opening words, taatee vaao na lagaee.

wordCard.voice: Taatee vaao, the hot wind: Guru Arjan's line says in the refuge of the Supreme Lord, it can't reach the one sheltered there; a protective circle stands on four sides.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the hot wind; the shabad opens taatee vaao na lagaee.

carryVoice: Your line: in his refuge. Shade and medicine, even while the wind still blows. Rest well.

sources.ref: Bilaval Mahalla 5 (taatee vaao na lagaee paarbraham sarnaaee), Ang 819
